# Accuracy is where the questions start {background-color="#00223e"}

## One number, six patients

The model for most of today is a random forest trained on 569 breast tumors.
Each tumor has 30 measurements taken from a biopsy image, and a label:
malignant or benign.

On 143 tumors it has never seen, the model is **95.8% accurate**. That means it
called 6 of them wrong.

The accuracy does not say which 6, or anything else we need in order to use the
model. Three questions are left open, and each one has a chart:

1. **How does it fail?** Which errors it makes, and what they cost.
2. **What is it using?** Which measurements drive the predictions.
3. **How sure is it?** Whether its confidence tells us anything.

# How does it fail? {background-color="#00223e"}

## The confusion matrix

::: {#55d02994 .cell execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=422 height=379 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


Read it by row. Of 53 malignant tumors, the model called 49 malignant and
4 benign. Of 90 benign tumors, it called 88 benign and 2 malignant.

## The two errors do not cost the same {.smaller}

A benign tumor called malignant leads to more tests. A malignant tumor called
benign is a cancer that goes untreated. Accuracy counts both as one error each.
The metrics below keep them apart.

| Metric | Question it answers | Here |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | Of all tumors, how many were called correctly? | 137 / 143 = **0.958** |
| Recall (malignant) | Of the real cancers, how many did the model catch? | 49 / 53 = **0.925** |
| Precision (malignant) | Of the tumors it called malignant, how many were? | 49 / 51 = **0.961** |

::: {.gw-box}
Which metric matters depends on which error is worse. For screening, a missed
cancer is the worse error, so recall is the number to report first.
:::

## The threshold is a choice

::: {#2452a827 .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=940 height=360 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


The model outputs a probability. The label comes from a cutoff, and 0.5 is only
the default. Each point on the ROC curve is one possible cutoff.

## What each threshold does to these 143 patients {.smaller}

| Call it malignant when P(malignant) is at least | Missed cancers | False alarms |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 (the default) | 4 | 2 |
| 0.4 | 3 | 3 |
| 0.3 | 1 | 7 |
| 0.2 | **0** | 9 |
| 0.1 | 0 | 20 |

Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2 finds all four missed cancers and sends
seven more healthy patients for further tests.

::: {.gw-box}
Choosing the threshold is not a modeling decision. It depends on what each error
costs, and the people who know those costs are usually not the ones who trained
the model. This table and the chart before it are how they take part in the choice.
:::

# What is it using? {background-color="#00223e"}

## Feature importance

::: {#35b04fb9 .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=771 height=369 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


A sorted bar chart, so the values are compared on a common scale. The top of the
list is three size measurements: area, perimeter and radius.

## Correlated features share the credit {.smaller}

::: {#a2f1a579 .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=810 height=348 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


Area, perimeter and radius describe the same nucleus, and their correlations are
0.98 to 0.99. The forest divides the credit among them. Shuffling any one of
them barely changes the accuracy, because the other two still carry the
information.

Both charts are correct. They answer different questions, so a feature
importance chart should say which definition it uses.

# Where does it fail, and does it know? {background-color="#00223e"}

## The error map

::: {#3311554e .cell execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=696 height=388 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


The projection is PCA, the method from Week 7. The six errors are not scattered.
They lie where the two classes meet, among tumors that resemble both.

## Confidence carries information

::: {#b1c0b3ce .cell execution_count=7}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=715 height=341 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


For most tumors the model answers close to 0 or close to 1. For the six it got
wrong, it answered between 0.29 and 0.76.

The probability tells us which predictions to trust less. This is the reason the
Week 12 server returns the probabilities and not only the label.

# The same questions for a text model {background-color="#00223e"}

## A review classifier {.smaller}

::: {#b5b55ae0 .cell execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=354 height=321 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


The data is IMDB movie reviews, each labeled positive or negative. TF-IDF turns
a review into word weights, as in Week 7, and logistic regression learns one
coefficient per word. The model is trained on 20,000 reviews.

**How does it fail?** It gets 141 of 1,000 wrong: 71 negative reviews called
positive, and 70 positive reviews called negative. Here the two errors cost the
same, and the matrix shows the model does not favor either class.

## What it uses: one coefficient per word

::: {#252af79f .cell execution_count=9}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-10-output-1.png){width=714 height=398 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


The model has learned which words signal praise and which signal complaint. It
adds up word weights. It does not read sentences.

## Read the errors {.smaller}

The quickest way to understand a text model is to read the cases it got wrong
while it was most sure.

> "This is, without a doubt, the most hilarious movie I've ever seen. Seriously,
> if the makers of this movie are ever discovered, they'll put guys like Jim
> Carrey out of a job."

A **negative** review. The model said P(positive) = **0.86**. The writer is
being sarcastic, and every weighted word in the review is a word of praise.

> "Great cult flick for MST-3K types: Richard Boone is a mess -- bad hair,
> arthritis ... about as good as a bad dino-flick can get"

A **positive** review. The model said P(positive) = **0.18**. The writer enjoys
the film for being bad, and the model counts "bad" twice.

No metric would have shown this. Reading a few confident errors is the text
version of the error map.

## Errors are concentrated where the model is unsure

::: {#bb297885 .cell execution_count=10}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-11-output-1.png){width=715 height=331 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


The model answers between 0.35 and 0.65 for 22% of the reviews. Those reviews
account for 55% of its errors.

An app that uses this model can treat that band differently, for example by
labeling the review "mixed" or by sending it to a person.

# Structure without labels {background-color="#00223e"}

## K-means and DBSCAN make different assumptions {.smaller}

::: {#eaeaeb11 .cell execution_count=11}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=906 height=292 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


When the data has no labels, the question is whether it has groups.

- **K-means** assumes round groups, and you tell it how many to find.
- **DBSCAN** finds groups as regions where points are packed closely. It decides
  the number itself, and it marks isolated points as noise.

HDBSCAN, which BERTopic used in Week 7, is DBSCAN without a fixed radius.

## DBSCAN on locations

::: {#717a27b4 .cell execution_count=12}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week13_ml_nlp_visualization_files/figure-revealjs/cell-13-output-1.png){width=888 height=398 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


DBSCAN finds 49 clusters and labels 1,041 sites as noise. The clusters are
metropolitan areas: New York and New Jersey (297 sites), the Bay Area (170),
Los Angeles (152). The gray sites are the highway network between them.

## The parameters are part of the result {.smaller}

The same 2,254 sites, with the neighborhood radius changed and nothing else:

| Radius | Clusters | Sites labeled noise | Largest cluster |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 km | 41 | 1,738 | 116 |
| 25 km | 49 | 1,041 | 297 |
| 50 km | 50 | 607 | 424 |
| 100 km | 20 | 188 | 1,093 |

At 100 km most of the eastern United States, from Florida to Massachusetts,
becomes one cluster.

::: {.gw-box}
There is no correct radius to discover. A cluster map should state its
parameters, for the same reason a histogram should state its bin width.
:::

# From the model to the user {background-color="#00223e"}

## Showing uncertainty in the client {.smaller}

A user never sees the confusion matrix. They see one prediction, in an app. What
the app shows decides whether they can tell a sure answer from an unsure one.

- **Label only.** A 0.99 and a 0.53 look identical.
- **Label and its probability.** Better, but for three or more classes it hides
  how close the second choice was.
- **The full distribution.** One bar per class. This is what the Week 12 server
  returns, and it is the display to prefer.

For the iris flower `(6.0, 2.7, 5.0, 1.7)`, the Week 12 server answers virginica
at 0.53, with versicolor at 0.47. In Block 3 you will send it a flower that comes
back at exactly 0.50 and 0.50, and decide what the app should show.

## One system, three parts

```text
Terminal 1   your Week 12 server      uvicorn server_skeleton:app --reload
Terminal 2   the Streamlit client     streamlit run app_live_predictions.py
Browser      sliders in, prediction and full distribution out
```

The client holds no model. Each prediction is a request to the server and a
response back, which is the loop from Week 11.

In the demo we stop the server while the app is open. The client should report
that the server is unreachable and keep running.

Your final project has this shape, with your own model in the server.

## Discussion {.gw-discussion}

**1.** For the tumor model, who should choose the threshold? What would you show
them so that they can?

**2.** The review classifier is wrong about sarcasm. Which of today's charts
would have revealed that, and which would not?

**3.** Your final project puts a model in front of a user. What will your app
show when the model is unsure?
